         12.      Under the PUA, the Commission possesses broad and exclusive authority over

utility rates and services, and must ensure that all rates imposed on the public are “just and

reasonable.” 23 This statutory standard grants the Commission significant discretion in the choice

of methodologies used to set or evaluate rates, so long as the ultimate results fall within a

permissible “zone of reasonableness” and reflect a balanced consideration of customer and

investor interests. 24 The law does not require the Commission to adopt any particular formula or

model; rather, the Commission’s responsibility is to craft rates that function reasonably in light of

utility operations, system conditions, and the evidentiary record before it. 25

        13.      This principle equally applies to the review of settlements: a stipulated resolution

is not binding on the Commission, and the Commission must independently ensure compliance

with the just-and-reasonable standard. 26

        14.      Because the Stipulation is contested, the Commission operates under 1.2.2.20(B)

NMAC. To approve the settlement, the Commission must find that the record demonstrates, by a

preponderance of the evidence, that:

              a. The agreement is the product of serious, informed bargaining among capable

                 parties representing diverse interests;

              b. The Stipulation, considered as a whole, produces rates that are fair, just, and

                 reasonable and serves the public interest; and

                                                DISCUSSION

        17.      The Stipulation contains twenty-eight separate provisions. For purposes of brevity,

the Commission does not discuss every provision individually in this Order, although it has

considered all provisions in evaluating the Stipulation as a whole.

        18.      The Commission's discussion is organized by the relevant provisions of the

recommended modifications contained in the Certification of Stipulation, summarizes the parties'

issues, the Commission considers whether the Stipulation, as modified, satisfies the standards

governing approval of a contested stipulation.

         Staff’s Exceptions

        25.      Staff contends that SPS’s post-filing revisions to its revenue deficiency,

depreciation expenses, 45 and SPS’s changed resource-adequacy information 46 confirm that its

        Commission Determination

        26.      The Commission’s FTY Rule defines and specifies the minimum data requirements

that must be filed to support an application for a rate change based on a future test-year period,

including a base period, an adjusted base period, a future test year period, and verifiable

information for the linkage data to allow the Commission to assess the validity of the information

contained in the future test year period. 48 The FTY contemplates that there may be changes to the

initial rate application, and sets out procedures to allow for those changes and notify the

Commission and parties. 49

        27.      The Commission disagrees that these changes, by themselves, establish that the

FTY is unreliable or no longer represents the test year that best reflects the conditions expected

when rates take effect. The FTY Rule expressly permits the use of estimated and projected data

and recognizes that the information underlying those estimates and projections may change during

the proceeding. By establishing a procedure for disclosing revisions, Rule 17.1.3.19 NMAC

contemplates that projections may evolve as additional information becomes available.

Accordingly, the Commission finds that the revisions to SPS’s revenue deficiency and depreciation

expense, or the changes to its resource-deficiency estimates, do not render the FTY unreliable or

         Staff’s Exceptions

        30.      Staff takes exception to the Certification of Stipulation's treatment of linkage data

and SPS's updating obligations under the Future Test Year Rule. 58 Staff argues that SPS was

        31.      Staff also asked that the Commission open a rulemaking to clarify a utility’s

        33.      The Commission disagrees with the Certification of Stipulation’s permissive

        34.      Applying the FTY Rule in this case presents a unique challenge because the rule

was designed for adjudicated future test year applications, where revisions are evaluated against

the utility's original application. That framework does not fit neatly where the parties have entered

into a comprehensive stipulation. A stipulated revenue requirement is no longer simply a forecast

derived from individual inputs but has become part of a negotiated package of concessions and

compromises. Under these circumstances, rather than focusing on the precision of the linkage

data, the Commission will review the Stipulation, as a whole, to determine whether the Stipulation

remains supported by the record and results in fair, just, and reasonable rates.
